question:
Let \(X_1,X_2,\ldots\) and \(X\) be random variables defined on the same probability space. Prove the following statements about modes of convergence:
(i) If \(X_n\to X\) almost surely, then \(X_n\to X\) in probability.
(ii) \(X_n\to X\) in probability if and only if every subsequence \(\{X_{n_k}\}\) contains a further subsequence \(\{X_{n_{k(i)}}\}\) such that \(X_{n_{k(i)}}\to X\) almost surely as \(i\to\infty\).
answer: Both statements are true. Part (i) follows by applying continuity from above to the events \(\bigcup_{n\ge m}\{|X_n-X|\ge \varepsilon\}\). Part (ii) follows by extracting from any subsequence a further subsequence with summable tail probabilities and applying the first Borel-Cantelli lemma; the converse is proved by contrapositive using part (i).
detailed_solution:
(i) Assume \(X_n\to X\) almost surely. Fix \(\varepsilon>0\). Define
\[
A_m=\bigcup_{n\ge m}\{|X_n-X|\ge \varepsilon\}.
\]
Then \(A_{m+1}\subseteq A_m\), and
\[
\bigcap_{m=1}^\infty A_m=\{|X_n-X|\ge \varepsilon \text{ infinitely often}\}.
\]
Since \(X_n\to X\) almost surely, for almost every \(\omega\), eventually \(|X_n(\omega)-X(\omega)|<\varepsilon\). Hence
\[
P\left(\bigcap_{m=1}^\infty A_m\right)=0.
\]
By continuity from above of probability,
\[
P(A_m)\downarrow 0.
\]
For every \(m\),
\[
P(|X_m-X|\ge \varepsilon)\le P(A_m),
\]
so \(P(|X_m-X|\ge \varepsilon)\to 0\). Therefore \(X_n\to X\) in probability.

(ii) First assume \(X_n\to X\) in probability. Let \(\{X_{n_k}\}\) be any subsequence. Then \(X_{n_k}\to X\) in probability as well. We construct a further subsequence recursively. Since \(P(|X_{n_k}-X|\ge 1/i)\to 0\) as \(k\to\infty\), for each \(i\ge 1\) we can choose \(k(i)>k(i-1)\) such that
\[
P(|X_{n_{k(i)}}-X|\ge 1/i)<2^{-i}.
\]
Let
\[
B_i=\{|X_{n_{k(i)}}-X|\ge 1/i\}.
\]
Then
\[
\sum_{i=1}^\infty P(B_i)\le \sum_{i=1}^\infty 2^{-i}<\infty.
\]
By the first Borel-Cantelli lemma,
\[
P(B_i\text{ infinitely often})=0.
\]
Thus, with probability one, only finitely many of the events \(B_i\) occur. Hence for almost every \(\omega\), there is \(I(\omega)\) such that for all \(i\ge I(\omega)\),
\[
|X_{n_{k(i)}}(\omega)-X(\omega)|<1/i.
\]
Therefore \(X_{n_{k(i)}}\to X\) almost surely.

Conversely, suppose every subsequence has a further subsequence converging almost surely to \(X\). We prove that \(X_n\to X\) in probability by contrapositive. Assume \(X_n\) does not converge to \(X\) in probability. Then there exists \(\varepsilon>0\) such that
\[
P(|X_n-X|\ge \varepsilon)
ot\to 0.
\]
Hence there exist \(\delta>0\) and a subsequence \(\{n_k\}\) such that
\[
P(|X_{n_k}-X|\ge \varepsilon)>\delta
\]
for all \(k\). Any further subsequence \(\{X_{n_{k(i)}}\}\) still satisfies
\[
P(|X_{n_{k(i)}}-X|\ge \varepsilon)>\delta
\]
for all \(i\), so it cannot converge to \(X\) in probability. By part (i), almost sure convergence would imply convergence in probability. Therefore no further subsequence of \(\{X_{n_k}\}\) can converge almost surely to \(X\), contradicting the assumed subsequence property. Thus \(X_n\to X\) in probability.

question: Suppose that \(X_{ij}=\alpha_i+\theta t_{ij}+\varepsilon_{ij}\), for \(i=1,\dots,a\) and \(j=1,\dots,b\), where \(\alpha_i\) and \(\theta\) are unknown parameters, \(t_{ij}\) are known constants, and \(\varepsilon_{ij}\) are independent random variables with mean \(0\). Assume that \(\sum_{i=1}^a\sum_{j=1}^b (t_{ij}-\bar t_{i\cdot})^2>0\), where \(\bar t_{i\cdot}=b^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^b t_{ij}\). Find explicit forms for the least squares estimators of \(\theta\) and \(\alpha_i\), \(i=1,\dots,a\).
answer:
Let \(\bar X_{i\cdot}=b^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^b X_{ij}\) and \(\bar t_{i\cdot}=b^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^b t_{ij}\). The least squares estimators are
\[
\hat\theta=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^a\sum_{j=1}^b (t_{ij}-\bar t_{i\cdot})(X_{ij}-\bar X_{i\cdot})}{\sum_{i=1}^a\sum_{j=1}^b (t_{ij}-\bar t_{i\cdot})^2}
=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^a\sum_{j=1}^b t_{ij}X_{ij}-b\sum_{i=1}^a \bar t_{i\cdot}\bar X_{i\cdot}}{\sum_{i=1}^a\sum_{j=1}^b (t_{ij}-\bar t_{i\cdot})^2},
\]
and
\[
\hat\alpha_i=\bar X_{i\cdot}-\hat\theta\,\bar t_{i\cdot},\qquad i=1,\dots,a.
\]
detailed_solution:
The least squares criterion is
\[
Q(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_a,\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^a\sum_{j=1}^b (X_{ij}-\alpha_i-\theta t_{ij})^2.
\]
For a fixed value of \(\theta\), differentiating \(Q\) with respect to \(\alpha_i\) gives
\[
\frac{\partial Q}{\partial \alpha_i}=-2\sum_{j=1}^b (X_{ij}-\alpha_i-\theta t_{ij})=0.
\]
Thus
\[
\hat\alpha_i(\theta)=\bar X_{i\cdot}-\theta\bar t_{i\cdot},\qquad i=1,\dots,a.
\]
Substituting this into the residuals gives
\[
X_{ij}-\hat\alpha_i(\theta)-\theta t_{ij}=X_{ij}-\bar X_{i\cdot}-\theta(t_{ij}-\bar t_{i\cdot}).
\]
Therefore the profile least squares criterion for \(\theta\) is
\[
Q_p(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^a\sum_{j=1}^b \{(X_{ij}-\bar X_{i\cdot})-\theta(t_{ij}-\bar t_{i\cdot})\}^2.
\]
Differentiating with respect to \(\theta\) and setting the derivative equal to zero yields
\[
\sum_{i=1}^a\sum_{j=1}^b (t_{ij}-\bar t_{i\cdot})\{(X_{ij}-\bar X_{i\cdot})-\hat\theta(t_{ij}-\bar t_{i\cdot})\}=0.
\]
Since \(\sum_{i=1}^a\sum_{j=1}^b (t_{ij}-\bar t_{i\cdot})^2>0\), the solution is unique and equals
\[
\hat\theta=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^a\sum_{j=1}^b (t_{ij}-\bar t_{i\cdot})(X_{ij}-\bar X_{i\cdot})}{\sum_{i=1}^a\sum_{j=1}^b (t_{ij}-\bar t_{i\cdot})^2}.
\]
Because \(\sum_{j=1}^b(t_{ij}-\bar t_{i\cdot})=0\), the numerator may also be written as
\[
\sum_{i=1}^a\sum_{j=1}^b t_{ij}X_{ij}-b\sum_{i=1}^a\bar t_{i\cdot}\bar X_{i\cdot}.
\]
Finally, substituting \(\hat\theta\) into \(\hat\alpha_i(\theta)\) gives
\[
\hat\alpha_i=\bar X_{i\cdot}-\hat\theta\bar t_{i\cdot},\qquad i=1,\dots,a.
\]

question:
Consider the likelihood function for a parameter \(\lambda>0\) based on Poisson count data,
\[
L(\lambda) \propto e^{-347\lambda}\lambda^{313}\left(1-e^{-\lambda}\sum_{i=0}^{3}\frac{\lambda^i}{i!}\right)^{13},
\]
with prior \(\pi(\lambda)=1/\lambda\). Using a latent-variable augmentation in which the factor \(1-e^{-\lambda}\sum_{i=0}^{3}\lambda^i/i!\) is represented by a Poisson tail probability, describe Gibbs sampling steps for sampling from the posterior distribution of \(\lambda\). Also give the Rao-Blackwellized estimator of the posterior mean of \(\lambda\) based on \(T\) Gibbs iterations. Use the Gamma distribution parameterized by shape and rate.
answer:
Introduce latent variables \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_{13}\), conditionally independent given \(\lambda\), with each \(Y_i\) following a Poisson\((\lambda)\) distribution truncated to \(\{4,5,\ldots\}\). At iteration \(t\):

1. Given \(\lambda^{(t-1)}\), sample independently
\[
Y_i^{(t)}\sim \operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda^{(t-1)})\mid Y_i^{(t)}\ge 4,\qquad i=1,\ldots,13.
\]
2. Given \(Y_1^{(t)},\ldots,Y_{13}^{(t)}\), sample
\[
\lambda^{(t)}\sim \operatorname{Gamma}\left(313+\sum_{i=1}^{13}Y_i^{(t)},\,360\right),
\]
where \(360\) is the rate parameter.

The Rao-Blackwellized estimator of \(E(\lambda\mid \text{data})\) is
\[
\widehat{\lambda}_{\mathrm{RB}}
=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^T E\left(\lambda\mid Y_1^{(t)},\ldots,Y_{13}^{(t)},\text{data}\right)
=\frac{1}{360T}\sum_{t=1}^T\left(313+\sum_{i=1}^{13}Y_i^{(t)}\right).
\]
detailed_solution:
The posterior density is proportional to the likelihood times the prior:
\[
\pi(\lambda\mid \text{data})\propto e^{-347\lambda}\lambda^{313}\left(1-e^{-\lambda}\sum_{i=0}^{3}\frac{\lambda^i}{i!}\right)^{13}\frac{1}{\lambda}
=e^{-347\lambda}\lambda^{312}\left(P_\lambda(Y\ge 4)\right)^{13},
\]
where \(Y\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda)\) and
\[
P_\lambda(Y\ge 4)=1-e^{-\lambda}\sum_{i=0}^{3}\frac{\lambda^i}{i!}.
\]

Introduce latent variables \(Y_1,
\ldots,Y_{13}\) whose joint augmented contribution is proportional to
\[
\prod_{i=1}^{13}\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{Y_i}}{Y_i!}\mathbf 1\{Y_i\ge 4\}.
\]
Summing each latent variable over \(y=4,5,\ldots\) recovers the factor \(P_\lambda(Y\ge 4)\), so the marginal posterior for \(\lambda\) is unchanged.

Given \(\lambda\), the full conditional distribution of each \(Y_i\) is therefore
\[
P(Y_i=y\mid \lambda,\text{data})=\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^y/y!}{P_\lambda(Y\ge 4)},\qquad y=4,5,
\ldots,
\]
which is a Poisson\((\lambda)\) distribution truncated below at \(4\).

Given the latent variables, the augmented posterior kernel for \(\lambda\) is
\[
e^{-347\lambda}\lambda^{312}\prod_{i=1}^{13}\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{Y_i}}{Y_i!}
\propto e^{-(347+13)\lambda}\lambda^{312+\sum_{i=1}^{13}Y_i}
=e^{-360\lambda}\lambda^{\left(313+\sum_{i=1}^{13}Y_i\right)-1}.
\]
Thus the full conditional is
\[
\lambda\mid Y_1,
\ldots,Y_{13},\text{data}\sim \operatorname{Gamma}\left(313+\sum_{i=1}^{13}Y_i,360\right),
\]
with shape-rate parameterization. Its conditional mean is
\[
E(\lambda\mid Y_1,
\ldots,Y_{13},\text{data})=\frac{313+\sum_{i=1}^{13}Y_i}{360}.
\]
Averaging these conditional means over Gibbs iterations gives the Rao-Blackwellized estimator
\[
\widehat{\lambda}_{\mathrm{RB}}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^T\frac{313+\sum_{i=1}^{13}Y_i^{(t)}}{360}
=\frac{1}{360T}\sum_{t=1}^T\left(313+\sum_{i=1}^{13}Y_i^{(t)}\right).
\]

question:
Suppose $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$, where $X_i$ are i.i.d. with common density $f_\theta$. Assume the usual regularity conditions so that the score has mean $0$ and variance equal to the Fisher information. For testing $H_0:\theta=\theta_0$ versus $H_1:\theta>\theta_0$, the locally most powerful score test rejects $H_0$ for large values of the score statistic
\[
T=S_n(\theta_0)=\sum_{i=1}^n \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log f_\theta(X_i)\right|_{\theta=\theta_0}.
\]
Using the central limit theorem, how should the critical value $c$ in the rejection rule $T>c$ be chosen for large $n$ so that the test has approximate level $\alpha$? Express your answer in terms of the Fisher information $I(\theta_0)$ for one observation.
answer:
Choose
\[
c\approx z_{1-\alpha}\sqrt{nI(\theta_0)},
\]
where $z_{1-\alpha}=\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha)$ is the $(1-\alpha)$ quantile of the standard normal distribution. Equivalently, if $z_\alpha$ denotes the upper-tail critical value satisfying $P(Z>z_\alpha)=\alpha$ for $Z\sim N(0,1)$, then $c\approx z_\alpha\sqrt{nI(\theta_0)}$.
detailed_solution:
Let
\[
s_{\theta_0}(X_i)=\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log f_\theta(X_i)\right|_{\theta=\theta_0}.
\]
Under the regularity conditions and under $H_0$, we have
\[
E_{\theta_0}[s_{\theta_0}(X_i)]=0,\qquad \operatorname{Var}_{\theta_0}(s_{\theta_0}(X_i))=I(\theta_0),
\]
where $I(\theta_0)$ is the Fisher information in one observation. Since the $X_i$ are i.i.d., the score statistic is
\[
T=S_n(\theta_0)=\sum_{i=1}^n s_{\theta_0}(X_i),
\]
so under $H_0$ it has mean $0$ and variance $nI(\theta_0)$. By the central limit theorem,
\[
\frac{S_n(\theta_0)}{\sqrt{nI(\theta_0)}}\Rightarrow N(0,1).
\]
Therefore, for large $n$,
\[
P_{\theta_0}(T>c)\approx P\left(Z>\frac{c}{\sqrt{nI(\theta_0)}}\right),\qquad Z\sim N(0,1).
\]
To make this probability approximately equal to $\alpha$, choose
\[
\frac{c}{\sqrt{nI(\theta_0)}}=z_{1-\alpha},
\]
where $\Phi(z_{1-\alpha})=1-\alpha$. Hence
\[
c\approx z_{1-\alpha}\sqrt{nI(\theta_0)}.
\]
source: Theoretical Statistics Topics for a Core Course

question: Explain how residual plots can be used to assess the goodness of fit and assumptions of a regression model.
answer: A residual plot displays residuals, typically \(r_i=y_i-\hat y_i\), against the predictor values, fitted values, or time/order. A regression model is supported when the residuals form a random cloud centered around 0, with roughly equal numbers of points above and below 0, no systematic trend or curvature, and approximately constant vertical spread. Patterns such as curves, clusters, outliers, or a funnel-shaped spread suggest lack of fit, nonlinearity, heteroscedasticity, dependence, or influential observations. Normality is not usually assessed from a residual-versus-fitted or residual-versus-predictor plot alone; it is better checked with a histogram or Q-Q plot of residuals.
detailed_solution:
For each observation, the residual is \(r_i=y_i-\hat y_i\), the difference between the observed response and the value predicted by the regression model. A residual plot places these residuals on the vertical axis and usually plots fitted values \(\hat y_i\), predictor values \(x_i\), or observation order on the horizontal axis.

If the regression model is appropriate, the residuals should behave like random errors. Thus, the plot should show points scattered randomly around the horizontal line \(r=0\). This indicates that the model is not systematically overpredicting or underpredicting in particular regions. The vertical spread should also be roughly constant across the horizontal axis, which supports the constant-variance assumption. In addition, there should be no clear curvature, trend, clusters, or other structure; such patterns would suggest that the functional form of the model is inadequate, for example that a linear model is being used for a nonlinear relationship.

A funnel shape, where the residual spread increases or decreases as fitted values or predictors increase, suggests heteroscedasticity. Extreme points may indicate outliers or influential observations. If residuals are plotted against time or observation order, serial patterns may indicate dependence or autocorrelation.

Therefore, a residual plot supports a good regression fit when it shows a random, patternless cloud centered near zero with roughly constant spread. Normality of errors is related to regression inference, but it is usually assessed more directly using a histogram or Q-Q plot of the residuals rather than a residual-versus-predictor plot alone.

question: Two identical boxes each contain $m$ parts, where $m\ge 2$ is an integer. Box A contains only first-class products. Box B contains exactly one first-class product, and its remaining $m-1$ parts are second-class products. One of the two boxes is selected at random with equal probability, and then two parts are drawn successively from the selected box without replacement. Given that the first part drawn is first-class, what is the probability that the second part drawn is also first-class?
answer: $\frac{m}{m+1}$
detailed_solution:
Let $A$ be the event that Box A is selected, $B$ be the event that Box B is selected, $F_1$ be the event that the first drawn part is first-class, and $F_2$ be the event that the second drawn part is first-class. We need $P(F_2\mid F_1)$.

Since the box is selected at random, $P(A)=P(B)=\frac12$.

If Box A is selected, all $m$ parts are first-class, so
\[
P(F_1\mid A)=1,\qquad P(F_2\mid F_1,A)=1.
\]
Thus $P(F_1\cap F_2\mid A)=1$.

If Box B is selected, exactly one of the $m$ parts is first-class, so
\[
P(F_1\mid B)=\frac1m.
\]
But after drawing that first-class part first, no first-class parts remain in Box B, hence
\[
P(F_2\mid F_1,B)=0,
\]
and therefore $P(F_1\cap F_2\mid B)=0$.

Using conditional probability and the law of total probability,
\[
P(F_2\mid F_1)=\frac{P(F_1\cap F_2)}{P(F_1)}.
\]
Now
\[
P(F_1\cap F_2)=P(A)P(F_1\cap F_2\mid A)+P(B)P(F_1\cap F_2\mid B)=\frac12\cdot 1+\frac12\cdot 0=\frac12,
\]
and
\[
P(F_1)=P(A)P(F_1\mid A)+P(B)P(F_1\mid B)=\frac12\cdot 1+\frac12\cdot \frac1m=\frac12\left(1+\frac1m\right).
\]
Therefore
\[
P(F_2\mid F_1)=\frac{\frac12}{\frac12\left(1+\frac1m\right)}=\frac{1}{1+\frac1m}=\frac{m}{m+1}.
\]

question: In factor analysis or latent variable models with loading matrix \(W\), rotational non-identifiability can occur because, for an orthogonal matrix \(R\), the transformation \(W \mapsto WR\) and \(z \mapsto R^Tz\) may leave the observed-data distribution unchanged. Name five standard constraints, conventions, or modeling choices commonly used to remove, reduce, or choose among these rotationally equivalent solutions.
answer:
Five common approaches are:
1. Impose an orthogonal-and-ordered loading convention, such as requiring \(W^T W\) to be diagonal with ordered positive diagonal entries, as in PCA/probabilistic PCA conventions.
2. Impose a lower-triangular loading matrix with positive diagonal entries.
3. Impose fixed zero constraints or anchor-variable constraints so that selected factors load on selected variables in a prespecified way.
4. Use sparsity-inducing constraints or priors on the loading matrix, such as lasso, spike-and-slab, or ARD-type priors, often together with ordering/sign conventions.
5. Use non-Gaussian independent latent variables, as in independent component analysis, which can identify components up to permutation and scaling/sign under suitable conditions.
A related practical convention is to choose a particular post hoc rotation, such as varimax, to select one interpretable representative from an equivalence class, although this is usually a convention rather than full statistical identifiability.
detailed_solution:
In a standard Gaussian factor model, if the latent factors have an isotropic distribution, replacing the loading matrix by \(WR\) and the latent vector by \(R^Tz\), where \(R\) is orthogonal, leaves the product \(Wz\) and hence the observed distribution unchanged. Therefore the orientation of the latent factor space is not identifiable without additional restrictions.

Several standard remedies are used. First, one may impose an orthogonal-and-ordered convention on the loading directions. Merely requiring \(W^T W=I\) is not enough, because \((WR)^T(WR)=I\) for every orthogonal \(R\). A stronger PCA-like convention is to require \(W^T W\) to be diagonal with distinct, ordered positive diagonal entries, or equivalently to align the columns with ordered principal directions. This leaves at most sign ambiguities.

Second, one may require the loading matrix to be lower triangular with positive diagonal entries. This fixes an ordering and orientation of the factors and is a common identification restriction in Bayesian and classical factor analysis.

Third, one may impose prespecified zero or anchor constraints, for example requiring certain variables to load only on particular factors. If enough valid constraints are imposed, rotations that violate those zeros are no longer allowed.

Fourth, sparsity-inducing penalties or priors, such as lasso, spike-and-slab, or ARD-type priors, can favor sparse loading patterns and thereby select a particular orientation. Sparsity alone does not universally guarantee identifiability, but under suitable structural conditions and often with sign or ordering conventions it reduces or removes rotational ambiguity.

Fifth, one may change the latent-variable model by assuming mutually independent non-Gaussian factors. In independent component analysis, non-Gaussianity breaks the rotational symmetry of the Gaussian latent space, giving identification up to the usual permutation and scale/sign indeterminacies under standard conditions.

Finally, post hoc rotations such as varimax are widely used to choose an interpretable representative from a rotational equivalence class. They are useful conventions, although they should not always be described as guaranteeing full identifiability of the underlying statistical model.

question:
Prove the following theorem about the marginal distribution of a multivariate normal vector:

Let \(\mathbf{Z}\) be a \(p\)-dimensional multivariate normal random vector, denoted \(\mathbf{Z}\sim N_p(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})\). For an integer \(k\) with \(1\le k<p\), partition \(\mathbf{Z}\) into two subvectors
\[
\mathbf{Z}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{Z}_1\\ \mathbf{Z}_2\end{bmatrix},
\]
where \(\mathbf{Z}_1\) is \(k\)-dimensional and \(\mathbf{Z}_2\) is \((p-k)\)-dimensional. Correspondingly, partition the mean vector and covariance matrix as
\[
\boldsymbol{\mu}=\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\mu}_1\\ \boldsymbol{\mu}_2\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11}&\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\\ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{21}&\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}\end{bmatrix},
\]
where \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_1\) is \(k\times 1\), \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11}\) is \(k\times k\), and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{21}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}^{\top}\). Prove that the marginal distribution of \(\mathbf{Z}_1\) is
\[
\mathbf{Z}_1\sim N_k(\boldsymbol{\mu}_1,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11}).
\]
answer: \(\mathbf{Z}_1\sim N_k(\boldsymbol{\mu}_1,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11})\).
detailed_solution:
Let
\[
\mathbf{B}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{I}_k&\mathbf{0}_{k\times(p-k)}\end{bmatrix},
\]
where \(\mathbf{I}_k\) is the \(k\times k\) identity matrix. Then \(\mathbf{B}\) selects the first \(k\) components of \(\mathbf{Z}\), so
\[
\mathbf{Z}_1=\mathbf{B}\mathbf{Z}.
\]

A standard closure property of the multivariate normal distribution says that if \(\mathbf{X}\sim N_n(\boldsymbol{\nu},\mathbf{V})\) and \(\mathbf{A}\) is a fixed \(m\times n\) matrix, then
\[
\mathbf{A}\mathbf{X}\sim N_m(\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\nu},\mathbf{A}\mathbf{V}\mathbf{A}^{\top}).
\]
Applying this property with \(\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{Z}\), \(\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{B}\), \(\boldsymbol{\nu}=\boldsymbol{\mu}\), and \(\mathbf{V}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\), we get
\[
\mathbf{Z}_1=\mathbf{B}\mathbf{Z}\sim N_k(\mathbf{B}\boldsymbol{\mu},\mathbf{B}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{B}^{\top}).
\]

Now compute the transformed mean:
\[
\mathbf{B}\boldsymbol{\mu}
=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{I}_k&\mathbf{0}\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\mu}_1\\ \boldsymbol{\mu}_2\end{bmatrix}
=\boldsymbol{\mu}_1.
\]
Similarly, compute the transformed covariance:
\[
\mathbf{B}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{B}^{\top}
=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{I}_k&\mathbf{0}\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11}&\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\\ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{21}&\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{I}_k\\ \mathbf{0}\end{bmatrix}.
\]
First,
\[
\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{I}_k&\mathbf{0}\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11}&\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\\ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{21}&\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11}&\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\mathbf{B}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{B}^{\top}
=\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11}&\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{I}_k\\ \mathbf{0}\end{bmatrix}
=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11}.
\]
Thus
\[
\mathbf{Z}_1\sim N_k(\boldsymbol{\mu}_1,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11}),
\]
which is exactly the marginal distribution of the first \(k\) components of \(\mathbf{Z}\).

question: Given a sample mean \(\bar{x}=24\), hypothesized population mean \(\mu_0=20\), sample standard deviation \(s=4.1\), and sample size \(n=9\), assume the population is approximately normally distributed. Use a one-sample right-tailed \(t\)-test at significance level \(\alpha=0.01\) to determine whether there is sufficient evidence to conclude that \(\mu>20\).
answer: Reject the null hypothesis. There is sufficient evidence at the \(\alpha=0.01\) level to conclude that \(\mu>20\).
detailed_solution:
We perform a one-sample right-tailed \(t\)-test. The hypotheses are
\[
H_0:\mu=20,\qquad H_a:\mu>20.
\]
The test statistic is
\[
t=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}}
=\frac{24-20}{4.1/\sqrt{9}}
=\frac{4}{4.1/3}
=\frac{12}{4.1}\approx 2.927.
\]
The degrees of freedom are
\[
df=n-1=9-1=8.
\]
For a right-tailed test with \(\alpha=0.01\) and \(df=8\), the critical value is approximately
\[
t_{0.99,8}=2.896.
\]
Since
\[
2.927>2.896,
\]
the test statistic falls in the rejection region. Therefore, we reject \(H_0\). There is sufficient evidence at the \(0.01\) significance level to conclude that \(\mu>20\).
source: Probability and Statistics for Engineers and Scientists

question:
Let \(X\) be a real-valued random variable, and suppose its moment-generating function \(M_X(t)=E(e^{tX})\) is finite for all \(t\) in some open interval containing \(0\). Prove the following results:

(a) \(M_X(t)\) has the Taylor expansion about \(0\)
\[
M_X(t)=1+\mu t+\mu_2'\frac{t^2}{2!}+\mu_3'\frac{t^3}{3!}+\cdots,
\]
for \(t\) in a neighborhood of \(0\), where \(\mu=E(X)\) and \(\mu_n'=E(X^n)\) for \(n=1,2,3,\ldots\).

(b) For every positive integer \(n\), the \(n\)th raw moment of \(X\) is
\[
E(X^n)=M_X^{(n)}(0).
\]
answer:
If the moment-generating function is finite on an open interval containing \(0\), then \(M_X\) is analytic in a neighborhood of \(0\). Hence its Taylor expansion is
\[
M_X(t)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{M_X^{(n)}(0)}{n!}t^n.
\]
Differentiating under the expectation gives \(M_X^{(n)}(0)=E(X^n)\). Therefore
\[
M_X(t)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{E(X^n)}{n!}t^n
=1+\mu t+\mu_2'\frac{t^2}{2!}+\mu_3'\frac{t^3}{3!}+\cdots,
\]
and \(E(X^n)=M_X^{(n)}(0)\).
detailed_solution:
Since \(M_X(t)\) is finite on an open interval containing \(0\), there exists \(a>0\) such that \(E(e^{tX})<\infty\) for every \(|t|<a\).

First note that this assumption implies that all raw moments of \(X\) are finite. Indeed, for any fixed positive integer \(n\), there is a constant \(C_n>0\) such that
\[
|x|^n\le C_n(e^{bx}+e^{-bx})
\]
for all real \(x\), where \(0<b<a\). Taking expectations gives
\[
E(|X|^n)\le C_n\{E(e^{bX})+E(e^{-bX})\}<\infty.
\]
Thus \(E(X^n)\) exists for every \(n\ge 1\).

For \(|t|<a\), the function \(M_X(t)=E(e^{tX})\) can be differentiated under the expectation sign. More precisely, if \(t\) is restricted to a smaller interval \(|t|\le b<a\), then derivatives of \(e^{tX}\) are of the form \(X^n e^{tX}\), and they are dominated by an integrable exponential bound involving \(e^{cX}+e^{-cX}\) for some \(b<c<a\). Hence, by dominated convergence,
\[
M_X^{(n)}(t)=E(X^n e^{tX}), \qquad |t|<a.
\]
In particular, evaluating at \(t=0\) yields
\[
M_X^{(n)}(0)=E(X^n e^{0})=E(X^n).
\]
This proves part (b).

Because \(M_X\) is finite on an open interval around \(0\), the same domination argument also implies that \(M_X\) is analytic in a neighborhood of \(0\). Therefore its Taylor expansion about \(0\) is
\[
M_X(t)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{M_X^{(n)}(0)}{n!}t^n
\]
for all \(t\) sufficiently close to \(0\). Using \(M_X^{(n)}(0)=E(X^n)\), we obtain
\[
M_X(t)=
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{E(X^n)}{n!}t^n.
\]
Since \(E(X^0)=1\), \(E(X)=\mu\), and \(E(X^n)=\mu_n'\) for \(n\ge 1\), this becomes
\[
M_X(t)=1+\mu t+\mu_2'\frac{t^2}{2!}+\mu_3'\frac{t^3}{3!}+\cdots.
\]
This proves part (a), and part (b) follows as shown above.
source: Schaums Outline of Probability and Statistics

question:
The Gaussian isoperimetric inequality states that for any measurable set $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ and any $\varepsilon > 0$, the standard Gaussian measure $\gamma_n$ satisfies
\[
\gamma_n(A_\varepsilon) \geq \Phi\left( \Phi^{-1}(\gamma_n(A)) + \varepsilon \right),
\]
where $A_\varepsilon = \{ x \in \mathbb{R}^n : \operatorname{dist}(x, A) < \varepsilon \}$ is the $\varepsilon$-neighborhood of $A$, $\Phi$ is the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution, and $\Phi^{-1}$ is its quantile function.

Prove that this implies the following Gaussian concentration inequality for Lipschitz functions: if $f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is $L$-Lipschitz with $L>0$, and $X \sim N(0, I_n)$, then for every $t \geq 0$,
\[
\mathbb{P}\left( |f(X) - M_f| \geq t \right) \leq 2 \exp\left( -\frac{t^2}{2L^2} \right),
\]
where $M_f$ is a median of $f(X)$, meaning that $\mathbb{P}(f(X) \leq M_f) \geq \frac12$ and $\mathbb{P}(f(X) \geq M_f) \geq \frac12$. You may use the standard bound $1-\Phi(u)=\Phi(-u)\le e^{-u^2/2}$ for $u\ge0$.
answer: The Gaussian concentration inequality follows by applying the Gaussian isoperimetric inequality to the sublevel set $A=\{x:f(x)\le M_f\}$ and the superlevel set $B=\{x:f(x)\ge M_f\}$. Since both sets have Gaussian measure at least $1/2$, their $\varepsilon$-neighborhoods have measure at least $\Phi(\varepsilon)$. The Lipschitz property implies that the complements of these neighborhoods contain the corresponding upper and lower tail events. Hence each one-sided tail is bounded by $1-\Phi(\varepsilon)\le e^{-\varepsilon^2/2}$, and setting $\varepsilon=t/L$ gives the desired two-sided bound.
detailed_solution:
Let $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ be $L$-Lipschitz with $L>0$, let $X\sim N(0,I_n)$, and let $M_f$ be a median of $f(X)$.

First consider the upper tail. Define
\[
A=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:f(x)\le M_f\}.
\]
Since $M_f$ is a median, $\gamma_n(A)=\mathbb{P}(f(X)\le M_f)\ge 1/2$. By the Gaussian isoperimetric inequality, for every $\varepsilon>0$,
\[
\gamma_n(A_\varepsilon)\ge \Phi\left(\Phi^{-1}(\gamma_n(A))+\varepsilon\right)\ge \Phi\left(\Phi^{-1}(1/2)+\varepsilon\right)=\Phi(\varepsilon),
\]
because $\Phi^{-1}(1/2)=0$ and $\Phi$ is increasing.

If $x\in A_\varepsilon$, then there exists $a\in A$ such that $\|x-a\|<\varepsilon$. Since $f$ is $L$-Lipschitz,
\[
f(x)\le f(a)+L\|x-a\|<M_f+L\varepsilon.
\]
Thus
\[
A_\varepsilon\subseteq \{x:f(x)<M_f+L\varepsilon\}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\mathbb{P}(f(X)<M_f+L\varepsilon)\ge \gamma_n(A_\varepsilon)\ge \Phi(\varepsilon),
\]
so
\[
\mathbb{P}(f(X)\ge M_f+L\varepsilon)\le 1-\Phi(\varepsilon)=\Phi(-\varepsilon)\le e^{-\varepsilon^2/2}.
\]

Now consider the lower tail. Define
\[
B=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:f(x)\ge M_f\}.
\]
Again, by the median property, $\gamma_n(B)\ge 1/2$. Applying the Gaussian isoperimetric inequality to $B$ gives
\[
\gamma_n(B_\varepsilon)\ge \Phi(\varepsilon).
\]
If $x\in B_\varepsilon$, then for some $b\in B$ we have $\|x-b\|<\varepsilon$, and hence
\[
f(x)\ge f(b)-L\|x-b\|>M_f-L\varepsilon.
\]
Thus
\[
B_\varepsilon\subseteq \{x:f(x)>M_f-L\varepsilon\}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\mathbb{P}(f(X)>M_f-L\varepsilon)\ge \Phi(\varepsilon),
\]
and hence
\[
\mathbb{P}(f(X)\le M_f-L\varepsilon)\le 1-\Phi(\varepsilon)=\Phi(-\varepsilon)\le e^{-\varepsilon^2/2}.
\]

Combining the two one-sided estimates yields, for every $\varepsilon>0$,
\[
\mathbb{P}(|f(X)-M_f|\ge L\varepsilon)
\le \mathbb{P}(f(X)\ge M_f+L\varepsilon)+\mathbb{P}(f(X)\le M_f-L\varepsilon)
\le 2e^{-\varepsilon^2/2}.
\]
For $t>0$, set $\varepsilon=t/L$ to obtain
\[
\mathbb{P}(|f(X)-M_f|\ge t)\le 2\exp\left(-\frac{t^2}{2L^2}\right).
\]
For $t=0$, the same inequality is trivial since the left-hand side is at most $1$ and the right-hand side is $2$. Therefore the stated Gaussian concentration inequality follows.

question:
Suppose that $X_1$ and $X_2$ are zero-mean sub-Gaussian random variables with parameters $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$, respectively, meaning that for all $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda X_i}\le \exp(\sigma_i^2\lambda^2/2)$ for $i=1,2$. A random variable $Y$ is called sub-exponential with parameters $(\nu,b)$ if $\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda(Y-\mathbb{E}Y)}\le \exp(\nu^2\lambda^2/2)$ for all $|\lambda|<1/b$.

(a) If $X_1$ and $X_2$ are independent, show that $X_1+X_2$ is sub-Gaussian with parameter $\sqrt{\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2}$.

(b) Show that, in general, without assuming independence, $X_1+X_2$ is sub-Gaussian with parameter at most $\sqrt{2}\sqrt{\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2}$.

(c) In the same setting as part (b), show that $X_1+X_2$ is sub-Gaussian with parameter at most $\sigma_1+\sigma_2$.

(d) If $X_1$ and $X_2$ are independent, show that $X_1X_2$ is sub-exponential with parameters $(\nu,b)=(\sqrt{2}\sigma_1\sigma_2,\sqrt{2}\sigma_1\sigma_2)$, under the above definition.
answer:
(a) $X_1+X_2$ is sub-Gaussian with parameter $\sqrt{\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2}$.

(b) Without independence, $X_1+X_2$ is sub-Gaussian with parameter at most $\sqrt{2}\sqrt{\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2}$.

(c) Without independence, the sharper bound $\sigma_1+\sigma_2$ also holds.

(d) If $X_1$ and $X_2$ are independent, then $\mathbb{E}[X_1X_2]=0$ and, for all $|\lambda|<1/(\sqrt{2}\sigma_1\sigma_2)$, $\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda X_1X_2}\le \exp(\sigma_1^2\sigma_2^2\lambda^2)$. Hence $X_1X_2$ is sub-exponential with parameters $(\nu,b)=(\sqrt{2}\sigma_1\sigma_2,\sqrt{2}\sigma_1\sigma_2)$.
detailed_solution:
Let the sub-Gaussian convention be $\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda X_i}\le e^{\sigma_i^2\lambda^2/2}$ for every $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$.

(a) If $X_1$ and $X_2$ are independent, then for every $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$,
\[
\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda(X_1+X_2)}=\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda X_1}\,\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda X_2}
\le \exp\left(\frac{\sigma_1^2\lambda^2}{2}\right)\exp\left(\frac{\sigma_2^2\lambda^2}{2}\right)
=\exp\left(\frac{(\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)\lambda^2}{2}\right).
\]
Therefore $X_1+X_2$ is sub-Gaussian with parameter $\sqrt{\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2}$.

(b) Without independence, apply Cauchy--Schwarz to $e^{\lambda X_1}$ and $e^{\lambda X_2}$:
\[
\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda(X_1+X_2)}
\le \left(\mathbb{E}e^{2\lambda X_1}\right)^{1/2}\left(\mathbb{E}e^{2\lambda X_2}\right)^{1/2}.
\]
Using the sub-Gaussian bounds at $2\lambda$ gives
\[
\left(\mathbb{E}e^{2\lambda X_1}\right)^{1/2}\left(\mathbb{E}e^{2\lambda X_2}\right)^{1/2}
\le \exp(\sigma_1^2\lambda^2)\exp(\sigma_2^2\lambda^2)
=\exp((\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)\lambda^2).
\]
Since
\[
(\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)\lambda^2=\frac{(\sqrt{2}\sqrt{\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2})^2\lambda^2}{2},
\]
$X_1+X_2$ is sub-Gaussian with parameter at most $\sqrt{2}\sqrt{\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2}$.

(c) Assume first that $\sigma_1,\sigma_2>0$. Let
\[
p=1+\frac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_1}=\frac{\sigma_1+\sigma_2}{\sigma_1},\qquad q=1+\frac{\sigma_1}{\sigma_2}=\frac{\sigma_1+\sigma_2}{\sigma_2}.
\]
Then $p,q>1$ and $1/p+1/q=1$. By Hölder's inequality,
\[
\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda(X_1+X_2)}
\le \left(\mathbb{E}e^{p\lambda X_1}\right)^{1/p}
\left(\mathbb{E}e^{q\lambda X_2}\right)^{1/q}.
\]
The sub-Gaussian bounds imply
\[
\left(\mathbb{E}e^{p\lambda X_1}\right)^{1/p}
\le \exp\left(\frac{p\sigma_1^2\lambda^2}{2}\right),\qquad
\left(\mathbb{E}e^{q\lambda X_2}\right)^{1/q}
\le \exp\left(\frac{q\sigma_2^2\lambda^2}{2}\right).
\]
Thus
\[
\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda(X_1+X_2)}
\le \exp\left(\frac{(p\sigma_1^2+q\sigma_2^2)\lambda^2}{2}\right).
\]
With the above choices,
\[
p\sigma_1^2+q\sigma_2^2
=\sigma_1(\sigma_1+\sigma_2)+\sigma_2(\sigma_1+\sigma_2)
=(\sigma_1+\sigma_2)^2.
\]
Therefore $X_1+X_2$ is sub-Gaussian with parameter at most $\sigma_1+\sigma_2$. If one of $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$ is zero, the same conclusion follows by a limiting argument, or directly because a zero sub-Gaussian parameter forces the corresponding centered variable to be almost surely zero.

(d) Since $X_1$ and $X_2$ are independent and centered, $\mathbb{E}[X_1X_2]=\mathbb{E}X_1\mathbb{E}X_2=0$. Let $s=\sigma_1\sigma_2$. For fixed $X_1$, the sub-Gaussian bound for $X_2$ gives
\[
\mathbb{E}\left[e^{\lambda X_1X_2}\mid X_1\right]
\le \exp\left(\frac{\sigma_2^2\lambda^2X_1^2}{2}\right).
\]
Hence
\[
\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda X_1X_2}
\le \mathbb{E}\exp\left(\frac{\sigma_2^2\lambda^2X_1^2}{2}\right).
\]
We now bound the square-exponential moment of $X_1$. For $a\ge 0$, using the Gaussian identity $e^{a x^2}=\mathbb{E}_Z e^{\sqrt{2a}xZ}$ with $Z\sim N(0,1)$ independent, the sub-Gaussian bound for $X_1$ implies, whenever $2a\sigma_1^2<1$,
\[
\mathbb{E}e^{aX_1^2}
=\mathbb{E}_Z\mathbb{E}_{X_1}e^{\sqrt{2a}ZX_1}
\le \mathbb{E}_Z e^{a\sigma_1^2Z^2}
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-2a\sigma_1^2}}.
\]
Taking $a=\sigma_2^2\lambda^2/2$ yields
\[
\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda X_1X_2}
\le \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-s^2\lambda^2}},\qquad |\lambda|<1/s.
\]
In particular, if $|\lambda|<1/(\sqrt{2}s)$, then $u=s^2\lambda^2<1/2$, and the elementary inequality $-\log(1-u)\le 2u$ for $0\le u\le 1/2$ gives
\[
\log \mathbb{E}e^{\lambda X_1X_2}
\le -\frac12\log(1-s^2\lambda^2)
\le s^2\lambda^2.
\]
Therefore
\[
\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda X_1X_2}\le e^{s^2\lambda^2}
=\exp\left(\frac{(\sqrt{2}s)^2\lambda^2}{2}\right)
\]
for all $|\lambda|<1/(\sqrt{2}s)$. Since $s=\sigma_1\sigma_2$, this is exactly the sub-exponential bound with $(\nu,b)=(\sqrt{2}\sigma_1\sigma_2,\sqrt{2}\sigma_1\sigma_2)$.

question: The amount of milk (in thousands of liters) dispensed by a milk booth located in a city is a random variable, \(X\), having a continuous uniform distribution with \(A = 7\) and \(B = 10\). Find the probability that on a given day, the amount of milk dispensed by this booth will be more than 7.4 thousand liters but less than 9.5 thousand liters.
detailed_solution:
For a continuous uniform distribution on the interval \([A, B]\), the probability density function is \(f(x) = \frac{1}{B-A}\) for \(A \le x \le B\). Given \(A = 7\) and \(B = 10\), we have \(f(x) = \frac{1}{3}\) for \(7 \le x \le 10\). The required probability is
\[
P(7.4 < X < 9.5)=\int_{7.4}^{9.5}\frac{1}{3}\,dx=\frac{9.5-7.4}{3}=\frac{2.1}{3}=0.7.
\]
Thus, the probability is \(0.7\).
source: Probability and Statistics for Engineers and Scientists

question:
In the first part of a game, a player tosses two fair coins. In the second part, the player rolls two fair dice, one fair die, or no dice, depending on the result of the coin toss, as follows:
- If the player tosses two heads, the player rolls two fair dice and is awarded a score equal to the absolute difference between the two numbers rolled.
- If the player tosses exactly one head, the player rolls one fair die and is awarded a score equal to the number shown on the die if that number is odd, and equal to half that number if it is even.
- If the player tosses two tails, the player is awarded a score of zero.

a) Show that the probability of obtaining a score of 1 is \(\frac{17}{72}\).
b) Find the probability of obtaining a score of not more than 1.
detailed_solution:
Let \(H\) be the number of heads obtained when the two fair coins are tossed. Then
\[
P(H=2)=\frac14,\qquad P(H=1)=\frac12,\qquad P(H=0)=\frac14.
\]

For part (a), compute the probability of a score of 1 by conditioning on \(H\).

If \(H=2\), the player rolls two fair dice and the score is \(|d_1-d_2|\). There are \(36\) equally likely ordered outcomes. The outcomes with absolute difference 1 are
\[
(1,2),(2,1),(2,3),(3,2),(3,4),(4,3),(4,5),(5,4),(5,6),(6,5),
\]
so
\[
P(\text{score}=1\mid H=2)=\frac{10}{36}.
\]

If \(H=1\), the player rolls one fair die. A roll of 1 gives score 1, and a roll of 2 gives score \(2/2=1\). No other die roll gives score 1. Hence
\[
P(\text{score}=1\mid H=1)=\frac{2}{6}.
\]

If \(H=0\), the score is automatically 0, so
\[
P(\text{score}=1\mid H=0)=0.
\]
Therefore, by the law of total probability,
\[
P(\text{score}=1)=\frac14\cdot\frac{10}{36}+\frac12\cdot\frac{2}{6}+\frac14\cdot 0
=\frac{10}{144}+\frac{1}{6}
=\frac{10}{144}+\frac{24}{144}
=\frac{34}{144}
=\frac{17}{72}.
\]

For part (b), we need \(P(\text{score}\le 1)\). Since the score is nonnegative, this is
\[
P(\text{score}\le 1)=P(\text{score}=0)+P(\text{score}=1).
\]
We already have \(P(\text{score}=1)=\frac{17}{72}\).

Now compute \(P(\text{score}=0)\). If \(H=2\), the two dice must be equal. There are 6 such ordered outcomes out of 36, so
\[
P(\text{score}=0\mid H=2)=\frac{6}{36}=\frac16.
\]
If \(H=1\), the possible scores are \(1,1,3,2,5,3\), depending on whether the die shows \(1,2,3,4,5,6\), so score 0 is impossible:
\[
P(\text{score}=0\mid H=1)=0.
\]
If \(H=0\), the score is always 0, so
\[
P(\text{score}=0\mid H=0)=1.
\]
Thus
\[
P(\text{score}=0)=\frac14\cdot\frac16+\frac12\cdot 0+\frac14\cdot 1
=\frac{1}{24}+\frac14
=\frac{7}{24}.
\]
Therefore
\[
P(\text{score}\le 1)=\frac{7}{24}+\frac{17}{72}
=\frac{21}{72}+\frac{17}{72}
=\frac{38}{72}
=\frac{19}{36}.
\]

question:
Let $X_{1}, X_{2}, \ldots$ be i.i.d. random variables from $N(\mu, \sigma^{2})$, where $\mu\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\sigma^{2}>0$. Let $w_{1}, w_{2}, \ldots$ be positive weights, and define weighted averages

$$Y_{n} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_{i} X_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_{i}}, \qquad n = 1, 2, \ldots.$$

a) Suppose $w_{k} = 1/k$ for $k = 1, 2, \ldots$. Show that $Y_{n} \overset{p}{\to} c$, identifying the limiting value $c$.

b) Suppose $w_{k} = 1/(2k-1)^{2}$. Show that $Y_{n} \Rightarrow Y$, giving the distribution of $Y$.
answer:
a) $c = \mu$.
b) $Y \sim N\left(\mu, \frac{2\sigma^{2}}{3}\right)$.
detailed_solution:
For any fixed $n$, $Y_n$ is a linear combination of independent normal random variables, so $Y_n$ is normal. Also,
$$\mathbb{E}[Y_n]=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n w_i\mathbb{E}[X_i]}{\sum_{i=1}^n w_i}=\mu,$$
and, by independence,
$$\operatorname{Var}(Y_n)=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n w_i^2\operatorname{Var}(X_i)}{\left(\sum_{i=1}^n w_i\right)^2}=\sigma^2\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n w_i^2}{\left(\sum_{i=1}^n w_i\right)^2}.$$

a) If $w_k=1/k$, then
$$\sum_{i=1}^n w_i=\sum_{i=1}^n \frac1i\to\infty,$$
while
$$\sum_{i=1}^n w_i^2=\sum_{i=1}^n \frac1{i^2}\leq \sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\frac1{i^2}<\infty.$$
Therefore
$$\operatorname{Var}(Y_n)=\sigma^2\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n i^{-2}}{\left(\sum_{i=1}^n i^{-1}\right)^2}\to 0.$$
Since $\mathbb{E}[Y_n]=\mu$, Chebyshev's inequality gives, for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$\mathbb{P}(|Y_n-\mu|>\varepsilon)\leq \frac{\operatorname{Var}(Y_n)}{\varepsilon^2}\to 0.$$
Thus $Y_n\overset{p}{\to}\mu$, so $c=\mu$.

b) If $w_k=1/(2k-1)^2$, then
$$\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} w_k=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(2k-1)^2}=\frac{\pi^2}{8},$$
and
$$\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} w_k^2=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(2k-1)^4}=\frac{\pi^4}{96}.$$
For finite $n$,
$$Y_n\sim N\left(\mu,\sigma^2\frac{\sum_{k=1}^n (2k-1)^{-4}}{\left(\sum_{k=1}^n (2k-1)^{-2}\right)^2}\right).$$
The variance converges to
$$\sigma^2\frac{\pi^4/96}{(\pi^2/8)^2}=\sigma^2\frac{\pi^4/96}{\pi^4/64}=\frac{2\sigma^2}{3}.$$
Hence the distribution functions, or equivalently the characteristic functions, of these normal random variables converge to those of
$$Y\sim N\left(\mu,\frac{2\sigma^2}{3}\right).$$
Therefore $Y_n\Rightarrow Y$ with $Y\sim N\left(\mu,2\sigma^2/3\right)$.
source: Theoretical Statistics Topics for a Core Course

question: Let \(X\) be the number of voters in a sample of \(n=400\) who favor the gasoline sales tax, and suppose we are testing \(H_0:p=0.60\) against alternatives \(p\ne 0.60\). Previously, the rule was to conclude that \(p=0.60\) when \(216<X<264\), that is, when \(217\le X\le 263\), and to reject \(H_0\) otherwise. Now suppose we use the rule to conclude that \(p=0.60\) when \(214<X<266\), that is, when \(215\le X\le 265\), and to reject \(H_0\) otherwise. Using the normal approximation with continuity correction, show that this new rule gives a smaller Type I error probability \(\alpha\), but increases the Type II error probability \(\beta\).
answer:
Under \(H_0:p=0.60\), \(X\sim \operatorname{Bin}(400,0.60)\), so \(\mu=400(0.60)=240\) and \(\sigma=\sqrt{400(0.60)(0.40)}=\sqrt{96}\approx 9.798\). For the new rule, the acceptance region is \(215\le X\le 265\), so the rejection region is \(X\le 214\) or \(X\ge 266\). Thus, using the normal approximation with continuity correction,
\[
\alpha_{\text{new}}=P(X\le 214\text{ or }X\ge 266\mid p=0.60)
=1-P(214.5\le X\le 265.5).
\]
Standardizing gives
\[
z_1=\frac{214.5-240}{9.798}\approx -2.60,\qquad z_2=\frac{265.5-240}{9.798}\approx 2.60.
\]
Therefore
\[
\alpha_{\text{new}}\approx 1-[\Phi(2.60)-\Phi(-2.60)]
=1-(0.9953-0.0047)=0.0094.
\]
For the previous rule, the acceptance region was \(217\le X\le 263\), so
\[
\alpha_{\text{old}}\approx 1-P(216.5\le X\le 263.5).
\]
Here
\[
\frac{216.5-240}{9.798}\approx -2.40,\qquad \frac{263.5-240}{9.798}\approx 2.40,
\]
so
\[
\alpha_{\text{old}}\approx 1-[\Phi(2.40)-\Phi(-2.40)]
=1-(0.9918-0.0082)=0.0164.
\]
Hence \(\alpha_{\text{new}}\approx 0.0094<0.0164\approx \alpha_{\text{old}}\). The new acceptance region \(215\le X\le 265\) contains the old acceptance region \(217\le X\le 263\). Therefore, for any alternative value \(p\ne 0.60\), the probability of accepting \(H_0\) is at least as large under the new rule as under the old rule. Thus the Type II error probability \(\beta\) increases.
detailed_solution:
Let \(X\) denote the number of voters in the sample who favor the gasoline sales tax. Under the null hypothesis \(H_0:p=0.60\), we have
\[
X\sim \operatorname{Bin}(400,0.60).
\]
Thus
\[
\mu=np=400(0.60)=240,
\qquad
\sigma=\sqrt{np(1-p)}=\sqrt{400(0.60)(0.40)}=\sqrt{96}\approx 9.798.
\]

The new rule concludes that \(p=0.60\) when \(214<X<266\). Since \(X\) is an integer, this means the acceptance region is
\[
215\le X\le 265.
\]
Therefore the rejection region is
\[
X\le 214 \quad \text{or}\quad X\ge 266.
\]
The Type I error probability is the probability of rejecting \(H_0\) when \(H_0\) is true:
\[
\alpha_{\text{new}}=P(X\le 214\text{ or }X\ge 266\mid p=0.60).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\alpha_{\text{new}}=1-P(215\le X\le 265\mid p=0.60).
\]
Using the normal approximation with continuity correction,
\[
P(215\le X\le 265)\approx P(214.5\le X\le 265.5).
\]
Standardizing,
\[
z_L=\frac{214.5-240}{9.798}\approx -2.60,
\qquad
z_U=\frac{265.5-240}{9.798}\approx 2.60.
\]
Hence
\[
P(214.5\le X\le 265.5)
\approx \Phi(2.60)-\Phi(-2.60).
\]
Using standard normal table values,
\[
\Phi(2.60)=0.9953,\qquad \Phi(-2.60)=0.0047.
\]
Thus
\[
P(214.5\le X\le 265.5)\approx 0.9953-0.0047=0.9906,
\]
and so
\[
\alpha_{\text{new}}\approx 1-0.9906=0.0094.
\]

For comparison, the previous rule accepted \(H_0\) when \(216<X<264\), i.e. when \(217\le X\le 263\). Its rejection region was \(X\le 216\) or \(X\ge 264\). Therefore
\[
\alpha_{\text{old}}=1-P(217\le X\le 263\mid p=0.60).
\]
Using continuity correction,
\[
P(217\le X\le 263)\approx P(216.5\le X\le 263.5).
\]
The corresponding standardized values are
\[
\frac{216.5-240}{9.798}\approx -2.40,
\qquad
\frac{263.5-240}{9.798}\approx 2.40.
\]
Therefore
\[
\alpha_{\text{old}}
\approx 1-[\Phi(2.40)-\Phi(-2.40)].
\]
Using \(\Phi(2.40)=0.9918\) and \(\Phi(-2.40)=0.0082\),
\[
\alpha_{\text{old}}\approx 1-(0.9918-0.0082)=1-0.9836=0.0164.
\]
Thus
\[
\alpha_{\text{new}}\approx 0.0094<0.0164\approx \alpha_{\text{old}}.
\]
So the new rule has a smaller Type I error probability.

Now consider the Type II error probability \(\beta\), which is the probability of failing to reject \(H_0\) when \(H_0\) is false. For a fixed alternative value \(p\ne 0.60\),
\[
\beta=P(\text{accept }H_0\mid p).
\]
The old acceptance region was
\[
217\le X\le 263,
\]
while the new acceptance region is
\[
215\le X\le 265.
\]
The new acceptance region contains the old acceptance region and also includes the additional possible outcomes \(X=215,216,264,265\). Therefore, for any alternative \(p\ne 0.60\),
\[
P(215\le X\le 265\mid p)\ge P(217\le X\le 263\mid p).
\]
Hence
\[
\beta_{\text{new}}\ge \beta_{\text{old}}.
\]
Since the new rule makes it easier to accept \(H_0\), it reduces \(\alpha\) but increases the probability of Type II error \(\beta\).

question: Given the hypotheses $H_0: \mu_A = \mu_B$ versus $H_1: \mu_A > \mu_B$ for a runs test, with significance level $\alpha=0.01$, suppose the test statistic is $V$, the observed total number of runs is $v=6$, and for sample sizes $n_1=9$ and $n_2=9$ the P-value is $P(V\le 6\mid H_0\text{ is true})=0.044$. What is the decision at the 0.01 significance level? Explain your reasoning.
answer: Do not reject $H_0$. There is insufficient evidence at the 0.01 significance level to conclude that $\mu_A>\mu_B$.
detailed_solution:
For a hypothesis test using the P-value approach, reject the null hypothesis $H_0$ when the P-value is less than or equal to the significance level $\alpha$. Here the given P-value is $0.044$, while the significance level is $\alpha=0.01$. Since
\[
0.044>0.01,
\]
the result is not statistically significant at the 0.01 level. Therefore, we do not reject $H_0: \mu_A=\mu_B$. The data do not provide sufficient evidence to support the alternative hypothesis $H_1: \mu_A>\mu_B$ at this significance level.

question:
Let \(V\) be a subset (in particular, it may be a subspace) of \(\mathbb{R}^n\). Define its orthogonal complement by
\[
V^{\perp}=\{x\in \mathbb{R}^n: v^{\top}x=0 \text{ for every } v\in V\}.
\]
Prove that \(V^{\perp}\) is a subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
answer: \(V^{\perp}\) is a subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
detailed_solution:
To prove that \(V^{\perp}\) is a subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^n\), we verify nonemptiness and closure under linear combinations.

First, the zero vector \(0\in\mathbb{R}^n\) belongs to \(V^{\perp}\), because for every \(v\in V\),
\[
v^{\top}0=0.
\]
Thus \(V^{\perp}\) is nonempty.

Now let \(x,y\in V^{\perp}\), and let \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}\). We show that \(\alpha x+\beta y\in V^{\perp}\). For any \(v\in V\), since \(x,y\in V^{\perp}\), we have
\[
v^{\top}x=0,\qquad v^{\top}y=0.
\]
Therefore,
\[
v^{\top}(\alpha x+\beta y)=\alpha v^{\top}x+\beta v^{\top}y=\alpha\cdot 0+\beta\cdot 0=0.
\]
Since this holds for every \(v\in V\), the vector \(\alpha x+\beta y\) is orthogonal to every vector in \(V\). Hence \(\alpha x+\beta y\in V^{\perp}\).

Therefore \(V^{\perp}\) is nonempty and closed under linear combinations, so \(V^{\perp}\) is a subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

question:
Let $Z$ be a real-valued random variable with median $M$, meaning that $\mathbb{P}(Z\le M)\ge 1/2$ and $\mathbb{P}(Z\ge M)\ge 1/2$. Let $\mathbb{E}Z$ denote its expectation whenever it is finite. Show that there exist absolute constants $c,C>0$ such that
$$c\,\|Z-\mathbb{E}Z\|_{\psi_2}\le \|Z-M\|_{\psi_2}\le C\,\|Z-\mathbb{E}Z\|_{\psi_2},$$
where
$$\|X\|_{\psi_2}=\inf\{t>0:\mathbb{E}\exp(X^2/t^2)\le 2\}.$$
answer:
The statement is true. One may take, for example,
$$C=1+\sqrt{2},\qquad c=(1+\sqrt{2})^{-1}.$$
detailed_solution:
We use two standard consequences of the given Orlicz norm. First, if $\|X\|_{\psi_2}=K<\infty$, then for all $t>0$,
$$\mathbb{P}(|X|\ge t)\le 2\exp(-t^2/K^2).$$
Indeed, this follows from Markov's inequality applied to $\exp(X^2/K^2)$, with the usual limiting argument if the infimum in the definition is not attained. Second, the Luxemburg norm associated with $\exp(x^2)-1$ satisfies the triangle inequality, and for a constant $a$,
$$\|a\|_{\psi_2}=\frac{|a|}{\sqrt{\ln 2}},$$
because $\exp(a^2/t^2)\le 2$ is equivalent to $t\ge |a|/\sqrt{\ln 2}$.

Let $\mu=\mathbb{E}Z$ and set
$$K=\|Z-\mu\|_{\psi_2}.$$ 
Assume first that $K<\infty$. If $K=0$, then $Z=\mu$ almost surely, hence the only median is $M=\mu$, and the desired estimates are trivial. Suppose $K>0$.

We first bound $|M-\mu|$ in terms of $K$. If $M\ge \mu$, then, since $M$ is a median,
$$\frac12\le \mathbb{P}(Z\ge M)=\mathbb{P}(Z-\mu\ge M-\mu)\le \mathbb{P}(|Z-\mu|\ge M-\mu).$$
Using the sub-gaussian tail bound gives
$$\frac12\le 2\exp\left(-\frac{(M-\mu)^2}{K^2}\right),$$
so
$$|M-\mu|\le \sqrt{\ln 4}\,K.$$ 
If $M\le \mu$, the same argument applied to the event $\{Z\le M\}$ gives the identical bound. Thus in all cases,
$$|M-\mu|\le \sqrt{\ln 4}\,K.$$ 
Therefore, by the triangle inequality,
$$\|Z-M\|_{\psi_2}\le \|Z-\mu\|_{\psi_2}+\|\mu-M\|_{\psi_2}.$$ 
Since $\|\mu-M\|_{\psi_2}=|\mu-M|/\sqrt{\ln 2}$, we obtain
$$\|Z-M\|_{\psi_2}\le K+\frac{\sqrt{\ln 4}}{\sqrt{\ln 2}}K=(1+\sqrt2)K.$$ 
Hence
$$\|Z-M\|_{\psi_2}\le (1+\sqrt2)\|Z-\mathbb{E}Z\|_{\psi_2}.$$ 

Conversely, let
$$K'=\|Z-M\|_{\psi_2}.$$ 
If $K'<\infty$, then $Z$ is integrable, so $\mu=\mathbb{E}Z$ exists. The random variable $Z-M$ has median $0$. Applying the same argument above to $Z-M$ gives
$$|\mathbb{E}(Z-M)-0|=|\mu-M|\le \sqrt{\ln 4}\,K'.$$ 
Then
$$\|Z-\mu\|_{\psi_2}=\|(Z-M)+(M-\mu)\|_{\psi_2}\le \|Z-M\|_{\psi_2}+\|M-\mu\|_{\psi_2}.$$ 
Thus
$$\|Z-\mu\|_{\psi_2}\le K'+\frac{\sqrt{\ln 4}}{\sqrt{\ln 2}}K'=(1+\sqrt2)K'.$$ 
Equivalently,
$$\|Z-M\|_{\psi_2}\ge (1+\sqrt2)^{-1}\|Z-\mathbb{E}Z\|_{\psi_2}.$$ 
Combining the two inequalities proves the claim with $C=1+\sqrt2$ and $c=(1+\sqrt2)^{-1}$.

question:
Prove the following result known as Young's theorem or Pratt's lemma. Let \((f_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}\), \((g_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}\), and \((G_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}\) be sequences of real-valued integrable functions on a measure space \((X,\mathcal A,\mu)\). Assume that:
(a) \(f_k(x)\to f(x)\), \(g_k(x)\to g(x)\), and \(G_k(x)\to G(x)\) for every \(x\in X\);
(b) \(g_k(x)\le f_k(x)\le G_k(x)\) for every \(k\in\mathbb N\) and every \(x\in X\);
(c) the limit functions \(g\) and \(G\) are integrable, and \(\int g_k\,d\mu\to \int g\,d\mu\) and \(\int G_k\,d\mu\to \int G\,d\mu\).
Prove that \(f\) is integrable and
\[
\lim_{k\to\infty}\int f_k\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu.
\]
Also explain why this theorem generalizes Lebesgue's dominated convergence theorem.
answer:
By applying Fatou's lemma to the nonnegative sequences \(f_k-g_k\) and \(G_k-f_k\), one obtains
\[
\int f\,d\mu\le \liminf_{k\to\infty}\int f_k\,d\mu
\quad\text{and}\quad
\limsup_{k\to\infty}\int f_k\,d\mu\le \int f\,d\mu.
\]
Hence \(\int f_k\,d\mu\to \int f\,d\mu\). The integrability of \(f\) follows from \(g\le f\le G\) together with the integrability of \(g\) and \(G\). The result generalizes dominated convergence because the fixed bounds \(-h\le f_k\le h\) in the dominated convergence theorem are replaced by varying lower and upper bounds \(g_k\le f_k\le G_k\) whose integrals converge correctly.
detailed_solution:
Since each \(f_k,g_k,G_k\) is measurable and the convergence is pointwise, the limit functions \(f,g,G\) are measurable. From \(g_k\le f_k\le G_k\) and pointwise convergence, we also have
\[
g\le f\le G.
\]
Because \(g\) and \(G\) are integrable, \(f\) is integrable as well: indeed,
\[
|f|\le |g|+|G|
\]
follows from \(g\le f\le G\), so \(\int |f|\,d\mu<\infty\).

Now apply Fatou's lemma to the nonnegative functions \(f_k-g_k\). Since \(f_k-g_k\ge0\) and \(f_k-g_k\to f-g\), Fatou's lemma gives
\[
\int (f-g)\,d\mu\le \liminf_{k\to\infty}\int (f_k-g_k)\,d\mu.
\]
Using integrability and linearity of the integral,
\[
\int (f_k-g_k)\,d\mu=\int f_k\,d\mu-\int g_k\,d\mu.
\]
Since \(\int g_k\,d\mu\to \int g\,d\mu\), we obtain
\[
\int f\,d\mu-\int g\,d\mu
\le
\liminf_{k\to\infty}\left(\int f_k\,d\mu-\int g_k\,d\mu\right)
=\liminf_{k\to\infty}\int f_k\,d\mu-\int g\,d\mu.
\]
Therefore
\[
\int f\,d\mu\le \liminf_{k\to\infty}\int f_k\,d\mu. \tag{1}
\]
Next apply Fatou's lemma to the nonnegative functions \(G_k-f_k\). Since \(G_k-f_k\ge0\) and \(G_k-f_k\to G-f\),
\[
\int (G-f)\,d\mu\le \liminf_{k\to\infty}\int (G_k-f_k)\,d\mu.
\]
Again by linearity,
\[
\int (G_k-f_k)\,d\mu=\int G_k\,d\mu-\int f_k\,d\mu.
\]
Since \(\int G_k\,d\mu\to \int G\,d\mu\),
\[
\liminf_{k\to\infty}\left(\int G_k\,d\mu-\int f_k\,d\mu\right)
=\int G\,d\mu-\limsup_{k\to\infty}\int f_k\,d\mu.
\]
Thus
\[
\int G\,d\mu-\int f\,d\mu
\le
\int G\,d\mu-\limsup_{k\to\infty}\int f_k\,d\mu,
\]
so
\[
\limsup_{k\to\infty}\int f_k\,d\mu\le \int f\,d\mu. \tag{2}
\]
Combining (1) and (2),
\[
\limsup_{k\to\infty}\int f_k\,d\mu
\le
\int f\,d\mu
\le
\liminf_{k\to\infty}\int f_k\,d\mu.
\]
Since always \(\liminf a_k\le \limsup a_k\), all three quantities are equal. Hence
\[
\lim_{k\to\infty}\int f_k\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu.
\]

Finally, the dominated convergence theorem is obtained as a special case. If \(|f_k|\le h\) for an integrable function \(h\), take
\[
g_k=-h,\qquad G_k=h
\]
for every \(k\). Then \(g=-h\), \(G=h\), and
\[
\int g_k\,d\mu=\int g\,d\mu,\qquad \int G_k\,d\mu=\int G\,d\mu
\]
for all \(k\). Thus Young's theorem applies and gives \(\int f_k\,d\mu\to\int f\,d\mu\). If the convergence and domination in the dominated convergence theorem hold only almost everywhere, one may modify the functions on the exceptional null set, which does not affect the integrals. Therefore Young's theorem/Pratt's lemma genuinely extends dominated convergence by allowing the lower and upper bounds to vary with \(k\), provided their integrals converge to the integrals of their limits.

question: A grayscale image is represented by an intensity matrix \(U_{\mathrm{orig}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\). Pixel values are known on a set \(K\subset\{1,\ldots,m\}\times\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and the missing pixel values are reconstructed subject to the constraint \(U_{ij}=(U_{\mathrm{orig}})_{ij}\) for all \((i,j)\in K\). Compare the qualitative behavior of two interpolation methods: one minimizing squared \(\ell_2\) variation, such as \(\sum_{(p,q)\sim(r,s)}(U_{pq}-U_{rs})^2\), and one minimizing total variation, such as \(\sum_{(p,q)\sim(r,s)}|U_{pq}-U_{rs}|\), where the sums are over neighboring pixels. What are the key differences in the reconstructed images produced by these two methods?
answer: Squared \(\ell_2\)-variation interpolation tends to produce very smooth reconstructions and often blurs sharp edges, because large differences between neighboring pixels are penalized quadratically. Total variation interpolation tends to preserve sharp edges better, because it penalizes jumps linearly through an \(\ell_1\)-type penalty on the discrete gradient. Thus, the \(\ell_2\) method usually gives smoother, more diffused images, while total variation gives more piecewise-smooth or piecewise-constant images with sharper transitions, though it may sometimes introduce staircasing artifacts.
detailed_solution:
The two methods impose different regularity preferences on the unknown image \(U\), while both keep the known pixels fixed by enforcing \(U_{ij}=(U_{\mathrm{orig}})_{ij}\) for \((i,j)\in K\).

For squared \(\ell_2\) variation, the regularization term has the form
\(\sum_{(p,q)\sim(r,s)}(U_{pq}-U_{rs})^2\),
which is a quadratic penalty on neighboring-pixel differences. Because the penalty grows quadratically, large jumps in intensity are strongly discouraged. As a result, the minimizer tends to spread changes gradually across the image. This produces a globally smooth reconstruction but can smear or blur true edges, since edges correspond to large local intensity differences.

For total variation interpolation, the regularization term has the form
\(\sum_{(p,q)\sim(r,s)}|U_{pq}-U_{rs}|\),
which is an \(\ell_1\)-type penalty on the discrete gradient. This penalty grows only linearly with the size of a jump, so a few large jumps are penalized less severely than under the squared \(\ell_2\) penalty. Therefore, TV minimization can maintain sharp transitions between regions. It often produces piecewise-smooth or piecewise-constant reconstructions, preserving edges better than squared \(\ell_2\) variation. A common drawback is possible staircasing, where smooth gradients are approximated by flat regions separated by jumps.

Hence the main qualitative difference is that squared \(\ell_2\) variation favors smooth diffusion and can blur edges, while total variation favors sparse gradients and better edge preservation.

question:
Consider the Bernoulli–Laplace model of diffusion with two urns, each containing exactly K balls, where K is a positive integer. Initially, urn 1 contains all K white balls and urn 2 contains all K black balls. At each step, one ball is chosen uniformly at random from each urn, independently conditional on the current state, and these two balls are swapped. Let X_n denote the number of white balls in urn 1 after n swaps. Then {X_n} is a Markov chain on the state space {0,1,...,K}.

(a) Determine the transition probabilities P_{ij}=P(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_n=i) for all i,j.

(b) Find the stationary distribution pi=(pi_0,pi_1,...,pi_K).

(c) Show that pi is a hypergeometric distribution and specify its parameters.
answer:
(a) For 0<i<K,
\[
P_{i,i-1}=\left(\frac{i}{K}\right)^2,\qquad
P_{i,i+1}=\left(\frac{K-i}{K}\right)^2,\qquad
P_{i,i}=\frac{2i(K-i)}{K^2},
\]
with all other transition probabilities from state i equal to 0. At the boundaries,
\[
P_{0,1}=1,\qquad P_{K,K-1}=1.
\]

(b) The stationary distribution is
\[
\pi_k=\frac{\binom{K}{k}^2}{\binom{2K}{K}},\qquad k=0,1,\dots,K.
\]

(c) This is the probability mass function of a hypergeometric distribution with population size N=2K, number of successes K, and sample size n=K. Thus, in standard notation,
\[
X\sim \operatorname{Hypergeometric}(2K,K,K).
\]
detailed_solution:
When X_n=i, urn 1 contains i white balls and K-i black balls. Since there are K white and K black balls in total, urn 2 contains K-i white balls and i black balls.

(a) To move from i to i-1, the swap must remove a white ball from urn 1 and replace it with a black ball from urn 2. The probability is
\[
\frac{i}{K}\cdot \frac{i}{K}=\left(\frac{i}{K}\right)^2.
\]
To move from i to i+1, the swap must remove a black ball from urn 1 and replace it with a white ball from urn 2. The probability is
\[
\frac{K-i}{K}\cdot \frac{K-i}{K}=\left(\frac{K-i}{K}\right)^2.
\]
The state remains i if the two chosen balls have the same color: either white from urn 1 and white from urn 2, or black from urn 1 and black from urn 2. Hence
\[
P_{i,i}=\frac{i}{K}\cdot\frac{K-i}{K}+\frac{K-i}{K}\cdot\frac{i}{K}=\frac{2i(K-i)}{K^2}.
\]
These formulas apply for 0<i<K. If i=0, urn 1 contains only black balls and urn 2 contains only white balls, so the next state is 1 with probability 1. If i=K, urn 1 contains only white balls and urn 2 contains only black balls, so the next state is K-1 with probability 1.

(b) The finite chain is irreducible for K>=1, so it has a unique stationary distribution. It is enough to verify detailed balance. For i=0,1,...,K-1, require
\[
\pi_i P_{i,i+1}=\pi_{i+1}P_{i+1,i}.
\]
Using the transition probabilities gives
\[
\pi_i\left(\frac{K-i}{K}\right)^2=\pi_{i+1}\left(\frac{i+1}{K}\right)^2,
\]
so
\[
\frac{\pi_{i+1}}{\pi_i}=\frac{(K-i)^2}{(i+1)^2}.
\]
Iterating from 0 to k gives
\[
\pi_k=\pi_0\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}\frac{(K-i)^2}{(i+1)^2}
=\pi_0\left(\frac{K!}{(K-k)!k!}\right)^2
=\pi_0\binom{K}{k}^2.
\]
Normalizing,
\[
1=\sum_{k=0}^K \pi_k=\pi_0\sum_{k=0}^K\binom{K}{k}^2.
\]
By Vandermonde's identity,
\[
\sum_{k=0}^K\binom{K}{k}^2=\sum_{k=0}^K\binom{K}{k}\binom{K}{K-k}=\binom{2K}{K}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\pi_0=\frac{1}{\binom{2K}{K}},
\]
and hence
\[
\pi_k=\frac{\binom{K}{k}^2}{\binom{2K}{K}},\qquad k=0,1,\dots,K.
\]

(c) If Y has a hypergeometric distribution with population size N, number of successes M, and sample size n, then
\[
P(Y=k)=\frac{\binom{M}{k}\binom{N-M}{n-k}}{\binom{N}{n}}.
\]
Taking N=2K, M=K, and n=K gives
\[
P(Y=k)=\frac{\binom{K}{k}\binom{K}{K-k}}{\binom{2K}{K}}
=\frac{\binom{K}{k}^2}{\binom{2K}{K}},
\]
which is exactly the stationary distribution pi_k. Thus the stationary distribution is Hypergeometric(2K,K,K).

question: The continuous random variable $T$ has probability density function $f(t)=16t^3+6t$ for $0<t<k$, and $f(t)=0$ otherwise, where $k>0$. Prove that there is only one possible value of $k$, and state its value.
answer: The only possible value is $k=\frac12$.
detailed_solution:
Since $f$ is a probability density function, its total integral over the real line must be $1$. As $f(t)=0$ outside $0<t<k$, we need
\[
\int_0^k (16t^3+6t)\,dt=1.
\]
Evaluating the integral gives
\[
\int_0^k (16t^3+6t)\,dt=\left[4t^4+3t^2\right]_0^k=4k^4+3k^2.
\]
Therefore $k$ must satisfy
\[
4k^4+3k^2=1.
\]
Let $u=k^2$. Since $k>0$, we have $u>0$. The equation becomes
\[
4u^2+3u-1=0.
\]
Factoring,
\[
4u^2+3u-1=(4u-1)(u+1)=0.
\]
Thus $u=\frac14$ or $u=-1$. Since $u=k^2>0$, $u=-1$ is impossible. Hence
\[
k^2=\frac14.
\]
Because $k>0$, it follows that
\[
k=\frac12.
\]
Thus there is exactly one possible value of $k$, namely $\frac12$.

question:
Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be a random sample from a normal distribution \(N(\theta,1)\), where the mean \(\theta\) is unknown and the variance is known to be 1. Suppose the prior distribution is \(\theta\sim N(0,1)\). Then the posterior distribution is
\[
\theta\mid X_1,…,X_n \sim N\left(\frac{n\bar X}{1+n},\frac{1}{1+n}\right),
\]
where \(\bar X\) is the sample mean.

(a) What is the Bayesian point estimate of \(\theta\) obtained from the posterior mean, median, or mode?
(b) Compare this Bayesian estimate with the maximum likelihood estimate \(\bar X\) in terms of finite-sample bias and asymptotic behavior.
answer:
(a) The Bayesian point estimate is
\[
\hat\theta_B=\frac{n\bar X}{1+n}.
\]

(b) The maximum likelihood estimate is \(\hat\theta_{MLE}=\bar X\), which is unbiased for \(\theta\). The Bayesian estimate is biased for finite \(n\), with bias
\[
\operatorname{Bias}(\hat\theta_B)=-\frac{\theta}{1+n}.
\]
However, the bias tends to 0 as \(n\to\infty\), and \(\hat\theta_B\) is asymptotically equivalent to \(\bar X\). In particular, it is asymptotically unbiased and consistent for \(\theta\).
detailed_solution:
The posterior distribution is normal:
\[
\theta\mid X_1,…,X_n \sim N\left(\frac{n\bar X}{1+n},\frac{1}{1+n}\right).
\]
For a normal distribution, the mean, median, and mode are all equal to its location parameter. Therefore, whether the Bayesian point estimate is taken as the posterior mean, posterior median, or posterior mode, the estimate is
\[
\hat\theta_B=\frac{n\bar X}{1+n}.
\]

For comparison, since \(X_i\sim N(\theta,1)\), the likelihood is maximized at the sample mean, so
\[
\hat\theta_{MLE}=\bar X.
\]
Because \(E_\theta(\bar X)=\theta\), the MLE is unbiased:
\[
\operatorname{Bias}(\bar X)=E_\theta(\bar X)-\theta=0.
\]

The Bayesian estimate can be written as
\[
\hat\theta_B=\frac{n}{n+1}\bar X.
\]
Thus
\[
E_\theta(\hat\theta_B)=\frac{n}{n+1}E_\theta(\bar X)=\frac{n}{n+1}\theta.
\]
Its finite-sample bias is therefore
\[
\operatorname{Bias}(\hat\theta_B)=E_\theta(\hat\theta_B)-\theta
=\frac{n}{n+1}\theta-\theta
=-\frac{\theta}{n+1}.
\]
So the Bayesian estimator is generally biased for finite \(n\), except when \(\theta=0\). However,
\[
\frac{n}{n+1}\to 1
\]
as \(n\to\infty\), so \(\hat\theta_B\) becomes asymptotically equivalent to \(\bar X\). Since \(\bar X\to \theta\) in probability, it follows that \(\hat\theta_B\to\theta\) in probability as well. Hence the Bayesian estimator is asymptotically unbiased and consistent.
source: Schaums Outline of Probability and Statistics

question:
Let \(\{(X_n^{(1)},\mathcal F_n), n\ge 0\}\) and \(\{(X_n^{(2)},\mathcal F_n), n\ge 0\}\) be martingales with respect to the same filtration \((\mathcal F_n)_{n\ge 0}\). Let \(a,b\in\mathbb R\). Prove the following statements:
1. \(\{(aX_n^{(1)}+bX_n^{(2)},\mathcal F_n), n\ge 0\}\) is a martingale.
2. \(\{(\max\{X_n^{(1)},X_n^{(2)}\},\mathcal F_n), n\ge 0\}\) is a submartingale.
3. \(\{(\min\{X_n^{(1)},X_n^{(2)}\},\mathcal F_n), n\ge 0\}\) is a supermartingale.
answer:
1. \(aX_n^{(1)}+bX_n^{(2)}\) is a martingale with respect to \((\mathcal F_n)\).
2. \(\max\{X_n^{(1)},X_n^{(2)}\}\) is a submartingale with respect to \((\mathcal F_n)\).
3. \(\min\{X_n^{(1)},X_n^{(2)}\}\) is a supermartingale with respect to \((\mathcal F_n)\).
detailed_solution:
Since \(X^{(1)}\) and \(X^{(2)}\) are martingales with respect to \((\mathcal F_n)\), each \(X_n^{(i)}\) is \(\mathcal F_n\)-measurable and integrable, and
\[
\mathbb E[X_{n+1}^{(i)}\mid \mathcal F_n]=X_n^{(i)},\qquad i=1,2.
\]

1. Define \(Y_n=aX_n^{(1)}+bX_n^{(2)}\). Then \(Y_n\) is \(\mathcal F_n\)-measurable and integrable because it is a finite linear combination of integrable \(\mathcal F_n\)-measurable random variables. Moreover, by linearity of conditional expectation,
\[
\mathbb E[Y_{n+1}\mid \mathcal F_n]
=\mathbb E[aX_{n+1}^{(1)}+bX_{n+1}^{(2)}\mid \mathcal F_n]
=aX_n^{(1)}+bX_n^{(2)}=Y_n.
\]
Thus \((Y_n,\mathcal F_n)\) is a martingale.

2. Define \(M_n=\max\{X_n^{(1)},X_n^{(2)}\}\). Since
\[
|M_n|\le |X_n^{(1)}|+|X_n^{(2)}|,
\]
\(M_n\) is integrable, and it is \(\mathcal F_n\)-measurable because \(X_n^{(1)}\) and \(X_n^{(2)}\) are. Also,
\[
M_{n+1}=\max\{X_{n+1}^{(1)},X_{n+1}^{(2)}\}\ge X_{n+1}^{(1)},
\qquad
M_{n+1}\ge X_{n+1}^{(2)}.
\]
Taking conditional expectations and using monotonicity gives
\[
\mathbb E[M_{n+1}\mid \mathcal F_n]\ge X_n^{(1)},
\qquad
\mathbb E[M_{n+1}\mid \mathcal F_n]\ge X_n^{(2)}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\mathbb E[M_{n+1}\mid \mathcal F_n]\ge \max\{X_n^{(1)},X_n^{(2)}\}=M_n.
\]
Hence \((M_n,\mathcal F_n)\) is a submartingale.

3. Define \(N_n=\min\{X_n^{(1)},X_n^{(2)}\}\). Again,
\[
|N_n|\le |X_n^{(1)}|+|X_n^{(2)}|,
\]
so \(N_n\) is integrable, and it is \(\mathcal F_n\)-measurable. Since
\[
N_{n+1}=\min\{X_{n+1}^{(1)},X_{n+1}^{(2)}\}\le X_{n+1}^{(1)},
\qquad
N_{n+1}\le X_{n+1}^{(2)},
\]
monotonicity of conditional expectation yields
\[
\mathbb E[N_{n+1}\mid \mathcal F_n]\le X_n^{(1)},
\qquad
\mathbb E[N_{n+1}\mid \mathcal F_n]\le X_n^{(2)}.
\]
Thus
\[
\mathbb E[N_{n+1}\mid \mathcal F_n]\le \min\{X_n^{(1)},X_n^{(2)}\}=N_n.
\]
Therefore \((N_n,\mathcal F_n)\) is a supermartingale.

question:
Let \(\{X_t:t\in T\}\) be a Markov stochastic process with finite or countably infinite state space \(S\). For \(s<\tau<t\), define the transition probabilities \(p_{ij}(s,t)=\mathbb{P}(X_t=j\mid X_s=i)\), assuming the relevant conditional probabilities are well-defined. Prove the Chapman--Kolmogorov equation
\[
p_{ij}(s,t)=\sum_{h\in S} p_{ih}(s,\tau)p_{hj}(\tau,t),\qquad i,j\in S.
\]
Equivalently, if \(P(s,t)=(p_{ij}(s,t))_{i,j\in S}\), prove that \(P(s,t)=P(s,\tau)P(\tau,t)\).
answer:
For every \(i,j\in S\) and \(s<\tau<t\),
\[
p_{ij}(s,t)=\sum_{h\in S}p_{ih}(s,\tau)p_{hj}(\tau,t).
\]
Thus, with the convention that rows are initial states and columns are terminal states, the transition matrices satisfy
\[
P(s,t)=P(s,\tau)P(\tau,t).
\]
detailed_solution:
Fix states \(i,j\in S\) and times \(s<\tau<t\). By the law of total probability over the finite or countable state space \(S\),
\[
\mathbb{P}(X_t=j\mid X_s=i)=\sum_{h\in S}\mathbb{P}(X_t=j, X_\tau=h\mid X_s=i).
\]
Using the multiplication rule for conditional probabilities,
\[
\mathbb{P}(X_t=j, X_\tau=h\mid X_s=i)
=\mathbb{P}(X_t=j\mid X_\tau=h, X_s=i)\mathbb{P}(X_\tau=h\mid X_s=i).
\]
Since \(\{X_t\}\) is Markovian, once the state at time \(\tau\) is known, the conditional distribution of the future state \(X_t\) does not depend on the earlier state \(X_s\). Hence
\[
\mathbb{P}(X_t=j\mid X_\tau=h, X_s=i)=\mathbb{P}(X_t=j\mid X_\tau=h)=p_{hj}(\tau,t).
\]
Also,
\[
\mathbb{P}(X_\tau=h\mid X_s=i)=p_{ih}(s,\tau).
\]
Substituting these two identities into the total probability expansion gives
\[
p_{ij}(s,t)=\mathbb{P}(X_t=j\mid X_s=i)
=\sum_{h\in S}p_{ih}(s,\tau)p_{hj}(\tau,t).
\]
This is the Chapman--Kolmogorov equation. If \(P(s,t)=(p_{ij}(s,t))_{i,j\in S}\), then the \((i,j)\)-entry of the matrix product \(P(s,\tau)P(\tau,t)\) is exactly
\[
\sum_{h\in S}p_{ih}(s,\tau)p_{hj}(\tau,t),
\]
so the matrix form is \(P(s,t)=P(s,\tau)P(\tau,t)\).
source: A First Course in Probability and Markov Chains

question:
Let \(X=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\) be a simple random sample from the shifted exponential distribution with unknown location parameter \(a\in\mathbb{R}\), whose density is
\[
f(x;a)=e^{-(x-a)},\quad x\ge a,
\]
and \(f(x;a)=0\) otherwise. Determine whether the Cramér-Rao regularity conditions are satisfied, and find the uniformly minimum variance unbiased estimator (UMVUE) of \(a\).
answer:
The Cramér-Rao regularity conditions are not satisfied. The UMVUE of \(a\) is
\[
\widehat a=X_{(1)}-\frac1n,
\]
where \(X_{(1)}=\min\{X_1,\ldots,X_n\}\).
detailed_solution:
The density can be written as
\[
f(x;a)=e^{-(x-a)}\mathbf 1_{\{x\ge a\}}.
\]
The support is \([a,\infty)\), which depends on the unknown parameter \(a\). Hence the usual Cramér-Rao regularity condition that the support be independent of the parameter fails. Equivalently, if one formally differentiates the log-density inside the support, one obtains \(\partial \log f(x;a)/\partial a=1\), whose expectation would be \(1\), not \(0\), showing that the usual interchange of differentiation and integration is invalid. Therefore the Cramér-Rao regularity conditions are not satisfied.

Now find the UMVUE. The joint density is
\[
\prod_{i=1}^n e^{-(x_i-a)}\mathbf 1_{\{x_i\ge a\}}
= e^{na}e^{-\sum_{i=1}^n x_i}\mathbf 1_{\{a\le X_{(1)}\}},
\]
where \(X_{(1)}=\min\{X_1,\ldots,X_n\}\). By the factorization theorem, \(T=X_{(1)}\) is sufficient for \(a\).

The distribution of \(T\) is obtained from
\[
P_a(T>t)=P_a(X_1>t,\ldots,X_n>t)=e^{-n(t-a)},\quad t\ge a.
\]
Thus
\[
f_T(t;a)=n e^{-n(t-a)}\mathbf 1_{\{t\ge a\}}.
\]
To show completeness, suppose \(E_a[g(T)]=0\) for every \(a\). Then
\[
\int_a^\infty g(t)n e^{-n(t-a)}\,dt=0,\quad \forall a.
\]
Multiplying by \(e^{-na}\) gives
\[
\int_a^\infty g(t)n e^{-nt}\,dt=0,\quad \forall a.
\]
Differentiating with respect to \(a\) yields
\[
-g(a)n e^{-na}=0,
\]
so \(g(a)=0\) almost everywhere. Hence \(T=X_{(1)}\) is complete.

Since \(T-a\sim \operatorname{Exp}(n)\), we have
\[
E_a[T]=a+\frac1n.
\]
Therefore
\[
\widehat a=T-\frac1n=X_{(1)}-\frac1n
\]
is unbiased for \(a\). Because it is an unbiased function of the complete sufficient statistic \(T\), the Lehmann-Scheffé theorem implies that \(X_{(1)}-1/n\) is the unique UMVUE of \(a\).

question:
Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with probability density function
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}a, & 0\le x\le 1,\\ 0, & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
\]
Find: (1) the constant $a$; (2) $P(-1<X\le 2)$.
detailed_solution:
Since $f(x)$ is a probability density function, it must satisfy
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx=1.
\]
Here $f(x)=a$ on $[0,1]$ and $0$ elsewhere, so
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx=\int_0^1 a\,dx=a.
\]
Thus $a=1$.

For the probability,
\[
P(-1<X\le 2)=\int_{-1}^{2} f(x)\,dx.
\]
Because the support of $X$ is contained in $[0,1]$, which lies inside $(-1,2]$, we get
\[
P(-1<X\le 2)=\int_0^1 1\,dx=1.
\]
Therefore, $P(-1<X\le 2)=1$.
source: 概率论与数理统计 (同济大学数学系) (Z-Library)

question:
An important factor in solid missile fuel is the particle size distribution. Significant problems occur if particle sizes are too large. Based on past production data, let the particle size \(X\) in micrometers have probability density function
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}
3x^{-4}, & x>1,\\
0, & \text{elsewhere}.
\end{cases}
\]
(a) Verify that \(f(x)\) is a valid probability density function.
(b) Find the cumulative distribution function \(F(x)=P(X\le x)\).
(c) Find the probability that a randomly selected particle exceeds 4 micrometers.
answer:
(a) \(f(x)\) is a valid probability density function.
(b) \[F(x)=\begin{cases}0, & x\le 1,\\ 1-x^{-3}, & x>1.\end{cases}\]
(c) \[P(X>4)=\frac{1}{64}\approx 0.015625.\]
detailed_solution:
To verify that \(f(x)\) is a valid probability density function, we check nonnegativity and total integral. For \(x>1\), \(3x^{-4}>0\), and elsewhere \(f(x)=0\), so \(f(x)\ge 0\) for all \(x\). Also,
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx=\int_1^\infty 3x^{-4}\,dx
=3\left[\frac{x^{-3}}{-3}\right]_1^\infty
=\left[-x^{-3}\right]_1^\infty
=0-(-1)=1.
\]
Thus \(f(x)\) is a valid density.

The cumulative distribution function is
\[
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\int_{-\infty}^x f(t)\,dt.
\]
If \(x\le 1\), then no probability mass lies at or below \(x\), so \(F(x)=0\). If \(x>1\), then
\[
F(x)=\int_1^x 3t^{-4}\,dt
=3\left[\frac{t^{-3}}{-3}\right]_1^x
=\left[-t^{-3}\right]_1^x
=-x^{-3}+1
=1-x^{-3}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
F(x)=\begin{cases}
0, & x\le 1,\\
1-x^{-3}, & x>1.
\end{cases}
\]
Finally,
\[
P(X>4)=1-F(4)=1-(1-4^{-3})=4^{-3}=\frac{1}{64}\approx 0.015625.
\]
source: Probability and Statistics for Engineers and Scientists

question: Let $X$ follow a Poisson distribution with mean $5$, i.e., $X\sim \operatorname{Poisson}(5)$. Calculate $P(X>5)$, rounding the result to four decimal places.
detailed_solution:
For $X\sim \operatorname{Poisson}(5)$, the probability mass function is
\[
P(X=x)=\frac{e^{-5}5^x}{x!},\qquad x=0,1,2,\ldots.
\]
Thus
\[
P(X>5)=1-P(X\le 5)=1-\sum_{x=0}^{5}\frac{e^{-5}5^x}{x!}.
\]
Compute the cumulative probability:
\[
P(X\le 5)=e^{-5}\left(1+5+\frac{5^2}{2!}+\frac{5^3}{3!}+\frac{5^4}{4!}+\frac{5^5}{5!}\right).
\]
The sum inside the parentheses is
\[
1+5+12.5+20.8333+26.0417+26.0417=91.4167.
\]
Therefore
\[
P(X\le 5)\approx e^{-5}(91.4167)\approx 0.6160.
\]
Hence
\[
P(X>5)=1-0.6160=0.3840.
\]
So, to four decimal places, $P(X>5)\approx 0.3840$.
source: Probability and Statistics for Engineers and Scientists

question:
A continuous random variable \(X\) has the probability density function \(f(x) = \begin{cases} c\left(1 - \frac{x}{8}\right), & 0 \le x \le 8, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}\)
(a) Find the value of the constant \(c\).
(b) Find \(P(X \ge 6)\).
(c) Find \(P(4 \le X \le 6)\).
detailed_solution:
For \(f(x)\) to be a probability density function, its integral over the real line must equal 1. Since \(f(x)=0\) outside \([0,8]\),
\[
\int_0^8 c\left(1-\frac{x}{8}\right)\,dx=1.
\]
Now
\[
\int_0^8 \left(1-\frac{x}{8}\right)\,dx=\left[x-\frac{x^2}{16}\right]_0^8=8-\frac{64}{16}=8-4=4.
\]
Thus \(4c=1\), so
\[
c=\frac14.
\]

For part (b), using \(c=\frac14\),
\[
P(X\ge 6)=\int_6^8 \frac14\left(1-\frac{x}{8}\right)\,dx
=\frac14\left[x-\frac{x^2}{16}\right]_6^8.
\]
Compute the bracket:
\[
\left(8-\frac{64}{16}\right)-\left(6-\frac{36}{16}\right)=4-\left(6-\frac94\right)=4-\frac{15}{4}=\frac14.
\]
Therefore
\[
P(X\ge 6)=\frac14\cdot \frac14=\frac{1}{16}.
\]

For part (c),
\[
P(4\le X\le 6)=\int_4^6 \frac14\left(1-\frac{x}{8}\right)\,dx
=\frac14\left[x-\frac{x^2}{16}\right]_4^6.
\]
Compute the bracket:
\[
\left(6-\frac{36}{16}\right)-\left(4-\frac{16}{16}\right)
=\left(6-\frac94\right)-(4-1)=\frac{15}{4}-3=\frac34.
\]
Hence
\[
P(4\le X\le 6)=\frac14\cdot \frac34=\frac{3}{16}.
\]

question: In a winter flu epidemic, researchers at a pharmaceutical company surveyed parents of babies to determine whether the company's new medicine improved recovery within two days. Among 120 babies who had the flu and were given the medicine, 29 were cured within two days. Among 280 babies who had the flu but were not given the medicine, 56 recovered within two days. At the 0.05 significance level, is there significant evidence that the medicine increases the two-day cure rate?
answer: No. Using a one-sided two-proportion z-test with hypotheses \(H_0:p_1=p_2\) and \(H_1:p_1>p_2\), the test statistic is \(z\approx 0.93\), which is less than the 0.05 upper-tail critical value \(1.645\). Equivalently, the one-sided p-value is about \(0.18\). Therefore, we fail to reject \(H_0\); there is not sufficient evidence at the 0.05 significance level to support the claim that the medicine is effective in increasing the two-day cure rate.
detailed_solution:
Let \(p_1\) be the true two-day cure rate for babies given the medicine and \(p_2\) be the true two-day recovery rate for babies not given the medicine. The company's claim is that the medicine increases the cure rate, so we test
\[
H_0:p_1=p_2,\qquad H_1:p_1>p_2.
\]
The sample proportions are
\[
\hat p_1=\frac{29}{120}=0.2417,\qquad \hat p_2=\frac{56}{280}=0.2000.
\]
Under \(H_0\), use the pooled proportion
\[
\hat p=\frac{29+56}{120+280}=\frac{85}{400}=0.2125.
\]
The standard error under the null hypothesis is
\[
SE=\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)\left(\frac{1}{120}+\frac{1}{280}\right)}
=\sqrt{0.2125(0.7875)\left(\frac{1}{120}+\frac{1}{280}\right)}\approx 0.04463.
\]
Thus the test statistic is
\[
z=\frac{\hat p_1-\hat p_2}{SE}
=\frac{0.2417-0.2000}{0.04463}\approx 0.93.
\]
For a one-sided test at \(\alpha=0.05\), the critical value is \(z_{0.95}=1.645\). Since \(0.93<1.645\), the statistic is not in the rejection region. Therefore, we fail to reject \(H_0\). The data do not provide significant evidence at the 0.05 level that the medicine increases the probability of recovery within two days.
source: Probability and Statistics for Engineers and Scientists

question:
The independent random variables $A$, $B$, and $C$ satisfy $A\sim \operatorname{Po}(1)$, $B\sim \operatorname{Po}(2)$, and $C\sim \operatorname{Po}(3)$. Let $V=A+B+C$.

a) State the distribution of $V$.

b) Calculate:

i) $P(V=3)$;

ii) $P(V\ge 3)$.

Give numerical answers to 3 significant figures where appropriate.
answer:
a) $V\sim \operatorname{Po}(6)$.

b) i) $P(V=3)=36e^{-6}\approx 0.0892$.

b) ii) $P(V\ge 3)=1-25e^{-6}\approx 0.938$.
detailed_solution:
The sum of independent Poisson random variables is also Poisson distributed, with parameter equal to the sum of the individual parameters. Hence
\[
V=A+B+C\sim \operatorname{Po}(1+2+3)=\operatorname{Po}(6).
\]

For $V\sim \operatorname{Po}(6)$,
\[
P(V=k)=\frac{e^{-6}6^k}{k!}.
\]

For part b(i),
\[
P(V=3)=\frac{e^{-6}6^3}{3!}=\frac{216e^{-6}}{6}=36e^{-6}\approx 0.0892.
\]

For part b(ii), use the complement:
\[
P(V\ge 3)=1-P(V\le 2).
\]
Now
\[
P(V\le 2)=P(V=0)+P(V=1)+P(V=2)
=e^{-6}+6e^{-6}+\frac{6^2e^{-6}}{2!}.
\]
Thus
\[
P(V\le 2)=(1+6+18)e^{-6}=25e^{-6},
\]
so
\[
P(V\ge 3)=1-25e^{-6}\approx 0.938.
\]
